title: Kaddish for the teachers
hookLine: a Kaddish praying for teachers, their students and their students' students

cards: Every teacher had a teacher. The fourth-grade teacher who read aloud with all the voices learned it from someone. So did the coach, and the grandmother at the kitchen table.

And who taught them? Somewhere back along that line is a stranger whose patience is still being passed along, though nobody remembers their name. Jewish prayer sets aside a moment for that whole invisible line.
It comes right after a few minutes of study, and it's one of the forms of the Kaddish.

teach.h: KADDISH: MAY THE NAME BE HALLOWED.
teach.b: The Kaddish is often thought of as the mourner's prayer.
In fact it comes in several forms, and all share a core, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in the age of the Talmud: may God's great name be made great and holy in the world.
The congregation answers: may God's great name be blessed forever.
The Kaddish d'Rabbanan, the Kaddish of the rabbis, is said after a group has studied rabbinic teaching together. In the morning service it comes at the end of yesterday's readings.
And it adds a paragraph no other Kaddish has.
It asks for blessing on Israel, and on the teachers, and on their students, and on all their students' students, and on everyone who studies Torah, here and in every place.

It asks for peace, grace, kindness and compassion, long life, enough to live on, and help from heaven. Notice how far it reaches: not just my teacher, but students of students, across places and generations.
Like every Kaddish, it's said only with a minyan, the quorum for communal prayer, and often mourners lead it.
The Talmud, in tractate Sotah, says the world is held up by the response to the Kaddish said after study. Learning isn't treated as private.
It ends with a prayer for everyone who carried it to you, and everyone you'll carry it to.

how: Kaddish d'Rabbanan is said in a minyan after a passage of rabbinic study, including in the morning service after the readings on the offerings; mourners often lead it, and the congregation answers.

o: start the next passage right away.
games.why: a group that studies together closes with the Kaddish of the rabbis, asking blessing for the teachers and everyone who studies.

practice: Bring back the face of one teacher who mattered to you, living or gone, and one thing they said or did that stayed.

Then widen the picture: their teacher behind them, a line going back further than you can see, and forward to the people you've taught, even a little. If you pray, ask God's peace for the whole line; if not, simply wish it to them.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for the teachers. The line runs back past every name, and forward through you. That's day five hundred fifty-two.
